citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $G$ be a complex affine algebraic group
([[def-rational-action-on-affine-variety]]).

**Unipotent subgroups.** A closed subgroup $U\subseteq G$ is **unipotent** if
every non-zero finite-dimensional rational $U$-module has a non-zero $U$-fixed
vector. This fixed-vector condition is the characterization used in Brion's
Example 1.22 (printed p. 8), and it is
the only form of the notion used in this pair. Equivalently, by the Lie–Kolchin
theorem, $U$ is unipotent in the standard sense that it admits no non-trivial
rational characters and all its elements are unipotent; this equivalence is
recorded as a sourced parenthetical companion to the definition (Brion Example
1.22 cites Lie–Kolchin) and is not used as a supplier anywhere in this pair, so
no edge to the higher-order unipotent/solvable page is introduced.

**Reductive and linearly reductive groups.** The group $G$ is **reductive** if
it has no non-trivial closed normal unipotent subgroup, and **linearly
reductive** if every finite-dimensional rational $G$-module is completely
reducible, i.e. a direct sum of simple $G$-submodules
([[def-completely-reducible-representation]], [[def-semisimple-module]]).

Over $\mathbf C$ the two notions coincide: every complex
reductive affine algebraic group is linearly reductive, and conversely a
linearly reductive $G$ has no non-trivial closed normal unipotent subgroup.
Both implications, together with the identity-component reduction below, are
proved in
[[thm-complete-reducibility-and-reynolds-operator-for-complex-reductive-group]];
this definition only records them for consumers of that theorem.

Both notions depend only on the identity component, in the sense that $G$ is
reductive if and only if $G^\circ$ is, and $G$ is linearly reductive if and
only if $G^\circ$ is; the passage from $G^\circ$ to the finite component group
for both notions is carried out in the same theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a
complex reductive affine algebraic group
([[def-reductive-and-linearly-reductive-over-c]]).

(i) Every finite-dimensional rational $G$-module is completely reducible, so
$G$ is linearly reductive.

(ii) Every rational $G$-module $V$ is a direct sum of simple submodules; the
invariant subspace $V^G$ therefore has a unique $G$-stable complement $V_G$,
the sum of all simple submodules on which $G$ acts non-trivially. The
projection $R_V:V\to V^G$ with kernel $V_G$ is the **Reynolds operator** of
$V$; it is $G$-equivariant, restricts to the identity of $V^G$, and is natural:
for every morphism $f:V\to W$ of rational $G$-modules one has
$R_W\circ f=f^G\circ R_V$, and if $f$ is surjective then so is
$f^G:V^G\to W^G$.

(iii) If $A$ is a commutative $G$-algebra on which $G$ acts by algebra
automorphisms and which is a rational $G$-module, then $R_A$ is $A^G$-linear:
$R_A(ab)=a\,R_A(b)$ for $a\in A^G$, $b\in A$.

(iv) When $K\subseteq G$ is a compact subgroup whose Zariski closure in $G$ is
all of $G$, the Reynolds operator of a finite-dimensional rational $G$-module
is the invariant average $R_V(v)=\int_K g\cdot v\,dg$ with respect to
normalized Haar measure; in particular $R_V(v)$ is the unique element of $V^G$
in the convex hull of the $K$-orbit of $v$.

derivations.claim: Since $N$ is $G$-stable, $g\cdot(v+N):=\rho(g)v+N$ is well-defined on $V/N$. Its restriction maps $V^G$ into $(V/N)^G$, and its kernel is $\ker(\pi|_{V^G})=V^G\cap N$ by the definition of the quotient.
Under A1 and the reductive hypothesis F1, apply F2 to the equivariant surjection $\pi$; it follows that $\pi^G:V^G\to(V/N)^G$ is surjective.

The displayed map is well-defined because changing $v$ by an element of $V^G\cap N$ leaves $v+N$ unchanged. It is injective by the kernel computation in step 1.1 and surjective by step 1.2, so it is the claimed canonical linear isomorphism.

Use natural units $c=\hbar=1$ on four-dimensional Minkowski space $M=\mathbb R^{1,3}$ with coordinates $x^0=ct,x^1,x^2,x^3$ and metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. Fix a complex affine algebraic group $G$ with no nontrivial closed normal unipotent subgroup, where unipotent means that every nonzero finite-dimensional rational module has a nonzero fixed vector; this is the reductive hypothesis. Fix a finite set $I$ of field species. For each $i\in I$, fix a finite-dimensional complex $\mathbb Z/2$-graded vector space $\Phi_i=\Phi_i^{\bar 0}\oplus\Phi_i^{\bar 1}$ with a homogeneous basis and its component parities, and an algebraic representation $\rho_i:G\to\operatorname{GL}(\Phi_i)$ preserving the grading. Include the declared spacetime-index action in $G$ or in its specified finite-dimensional representation data.

For the field interpretation, fix a finite Grassmann coefficient algebra $\mathcal G=\Lambda_{\mathbb C}(\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_s)$, $s\geq0$, with its usual grading by generator degree modulo two. A field configuration assigns to each homogeneous component of parity $\bar p$ a function $M\to\mathcal G_{\bar p}$ whose coefficient at each exterior monomial is smooth; spacetime derivatives are taken coefficientwise. Evaluation of a polynomial on an $r$-jet means the parity-preserving algebra homomorphism that sends each polynomial coordinate to the corresponding field component or derivative at that point.

Fix a derivative cutoff $r\geq0$, a maximum polynomial field degree $q\geq0$, and a rational engineering weight $\Delta_i$ for each field species. A derivative $\partial_\mu$ has engineering weight one, and an $s$-jet generator is a component of $\partial_{\mu_1}\cdots\partial_{\mu_s}\phi_i(x)$ for $0\leq s\leq r$. If covariant derivatives are used, their finite jet generators and $G$-action are included explicitly in the same data. Let $J_r$ be the resulting finite-dimensional $\mathbb Z/2$-graded vector space with its specified algebraic representation $\rho_r:G\to\operatorname{GL}(J_r)$, required to preserve the grading and the assigned engineering weights. Its polynomial algebra is the supercommutative algebra $P_r=\operatorname{Sym}(J_{r,\bar 0}^{*})\otimes\Lambda(J_{r,\bar 1}^{*})$: even generators commute and odd generators anticommute. The induced left $G$-action on $P_r$ is $(g\cdot f)(z)=f(\rho_r(g^{-1})z)$ for $g\in G$, $f\in P_r$, and $z\in J_r$. For a fixed weight $D\in\mathbb Q$, let $P_{r,q,D}$ be the complex span of monomials of total engineering weight $D$ and total polynomial degree at most $q$.

A local operator in this finite-order data is an element of $P_{r,q,D}$ evaluated at $x$ on the $r$-jet of the fields. A scalar operator invariant under the declared symmetries is an element of $V_{r,q,D}=P_{r,q,D}^{G}$. Engineering dimension means this assigned mass weight; it is not a statement about an observed quantity. In four dimensions a term with operator $\mathcal O_D$ has the convention $C\mathcal O_D/\Lambda^{D-4}$, where $\Lambda$ has mass dimension one and $C$ is dimensionless. Reality conditions, when required for a real action, are additional conjugation data on $V_{r,q,D}$.

derivations.claim: If $n=0$, the polynomial algebra consists only of constants, so its degree-at-most-$q$ subspace has dimension at most one. If $n>0$, every monomial is indexed by an exponent vector $(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$ with $0\leq a_j\leq q$ for each $j$, since $\sum_j a_j\leq q$; hence the full degree-at-most-$q$ algebra is spanned by at most $(q+1)^n$ monomials. The exterior generators only reduce this finite set because their exponents are restricted to $0$ or $1$.

The subspace $P_{q,D}$ is spanned by the subset of those finitely many monomials whose assigned weights sum to $D$, so it is finite-dimensional; if no monomial has weight $D$, it is the zero space. The invariant vectors $P_{q,D}^{G}$ form a linear subspace of $P_{q,D}$ because the action preserves parity and weight, and every subspace of a finite-dimensional vector space is finite-dimensional.

Fix a finite jet order $r$, maximum polynomial field degree $q$, engineering weight $D$, finite field-species list, coefficient field $\mathbb C$, and complex reductive affine algebraic group $G$ with the finite-dimensional rational action specified on the jet generators, including the declared spacetime-index symmetries. Let $W_D$ be the finite-dimensional space of all local polynomials of weight $D$ and degree at most $q$, before imposing $G$-invariance, and let $V_D=W_D^G$ be its invariant scalar subspace. An admitted raw relation space is a specified $G$-stable linear subspace $\widetilde R_D\leq W_D$, given by explicit linear identities among the chosen polynomials. Its invariant part is $R_D=\widetilde R_D\cap V_D$. Any action, boundary, or observable interpretation of the selected identities is extra mathematical data and must be stated with the result that verifies it.

The finite-order invariant operator-basis quotient is

$$
\mathcal Q_D:=V_D/R_D.
$$

Two invariant operators represent the same class exactly when their difference lies in $R_D$. An operator basis is any finite list of representatives in $V_D$ of a vector-space basis of $\mathcal Q_D$. The quotient records precisely the declared relation space; it does not assert that every relation relevant to an arbitrary EFT, observable, or infinite operator tower has been included.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $G$ be a complex reductive affine algebraic group, let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space with an algebraic representation $\rho:G\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$, and let $N\leq V$ be a linear subspace satisfying $\rho(g)N=N$ for every $g\in G$. Define $V^G=\{v\in V:\rho(g)v=v\text{ for all }g\in G\}$, give $V/N$ the induced representation, and let $\pi:V\to V/N$ be the quotient map. Then the restriction $\pi^G:V^G\to(V/N)^G$ is surjective and has kernel $V^G\cap N$. Consequently the map

$$
V^G/(V^G\cap N)\longrightarrow(V/N)^G,\qquad v+(V^G\cap N)\longmapsto v+N
$$

is a canonical complex-linear isomorphism.

derivations.claim: The quotient map $W_D\to W_D/\widetilde R_D$ is equivariant because $\widetilde R_D$ is $G$-stable. By F1 its source is a finite-dimensional rational module, so under A1 we can apply F3 and conclude that its restriction to invariants is surjective.

An admitted integration-by-parts density is $\partial_\mu J^\mu$ with compactly supported $J^\mu$. Its action integral is zero by A2, so adding such a density does not change the action functional under the stated boundary convention.

By A3 and the admissibility condition in A4, the first variation of $S_0$ in direction $-\epsilon^kF$ is $-\epsilon^k\mathcal I(F^a\mathcal E_a^{(0)})$. The formal Taylor terms of degree at least two in the displacement have powers at least $\epsilon^{2k}$, which are in $O(\epsilon^{k+1})$ because $k\geq1$.

To construct a formal inverse through order $N$, use A4 and seek $\Phi_k=\operatorname{id}+\sum_{m=k}^N\epsilon^mH_m$. Because $F$ is smooth in finitely many jet coordinates, each coefficient of $F(\Phi_k(\phi))$ through order $N$ is defined by a finite Taylor expansion. At order $k$, the coefficient of $\Psi_k\circ\Phi_k-\operatorname{id}$ is $H_k-F$, so choose $H_k=F$. At each subsequent order $m$, that coefficient is $H_m$ plus an expression determined by the previously chosen $H_k,\ldots,H_{m-1}$; choosing $H_m$ as its negative cancels it. The recursion is finite, and every coefficient depends on finitely many jets, so it yields a local right inverse modulo $\epsilon^{N+1}$. The same recursion gives a left inverse, and a left and right inverse of one map agree; thus $\Psi_k$ is formally invertible.

The kernel of the restricted invariant map is $W_D^G\cap\widetilde R_D=R_D$. By F2, its domain modulo this kernel is exactly $\mathcal Q_D$, so the first isomorphism theorem gives the canonical isomorphism $\mathcal Q_D\cong(W_D/\widetilde R_D)^G$ and fixes the quotient's declared relation scope.

For each $j\geq1$, substituting $\phi-\epsilon^kF$ into $\epsilon^jS_j$ changes it first at degree $\epsilon^{j+k}$, at least $\epsilon^{k+1}$. Combining this with step 1.3 gives the displayed expansion for $S_\epsilon\circ\Psi_k$.

If the order-$k$ action contains $+\epsilon^k\mathcal I(F^a\mathcal E_a^{(0)})$, the negative term in step 2.2 cancels it, while the substitutions in all $S_j$ with $j\geq1$ begin above order $k$. Step 1.4 makes this an allowed invertible local field redefinition; its induced higher-order terms remain part of the transformed truncated action. No off-shell or quantum-measure conclusion follows from this action-level calculation.

Burgess (21)–(26), Neubert (27)–(29) and CPV (3.2) checked at their exact limited scopes.

Fix the field data and Minkowski convention from the earlier finite-jet definition, an integer truncation order $N\geq0$, and the truncated coefficient ring $R_N=\mathbb C[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^{N+1})$. For each regulator label $\rho$, let $X_\rho=X_\rho^{\bar 0}\oplus X_\rho^{\bar 1}$ be a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Z/2$-graded complex vector space of field-mode components, with $n_0=\dim_{\mathbb C}X_\rho^{\bar 0}$ and $n_1=\dim_{\mathbb C}X_\rho^{\bar 1}$. Choose even coordinates $q^1,\ldots,q^{n_0}$ and a basis of $X_\rho^{\bar 1}$ whose dual odd coordinate generators are $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_{n_1}\in(X_\rho^{\bar 1})^*$. Choose a real integration contour $\Gamma_\rho$ in the underlying real space of $X_\rho^{\bar 0}$ and a specified complex-linear functional $\ell_\rho$ on a specified complex algebra $\mathcal C_\rho$ of coefficient functions on $\Gamma_\rho$. The domain $\mathcal C_\rho$ must contain every coefficient function to which $\ell_\rho$ is applied. In an actual integral, $\ell_\rho(f)=\int_{\Gamma_\rho}f\,d\nu_\rho$ for a stated measure $\nu_\rho$ and the coefficients must be integrable; in a formal perturbative integral, $\ell_\rho$ is the stated coefficientwise linear functional and its domain is part of the datum.

The odd-coordinate algebra is the finite exterior algebra $\Lambda(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_{n_1})$, where $\xi_a\xi_b=-\xi_b\xi_a$ and $\xi_a^2=0$. Put $\mathcal H_\rho=\mathcal C_\rho\otimes\Lambda(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_{n_1})$ with graded tensor-product multiplication. For an ordered subset $I=\{i_1<\cdots<i_k\}$, write $\xi_I=\xi_{i_1}\cdots\xi_{i_k}$, and set $\xi_\varnothing=1$. Every field-coordinate expression is a finite sum $H=\sum_I f_I\xi_I$. Define the normalized odd-coordinate integration functional by
$$
\mathcal B_\rho(H)=f_{\{1,\ldots,n_1\}},\qquad \mathcal B_\rho(\xi_1\cdots\xi_{n_1})=1.
$$
If $n_1=0$, $\mathcal B_\rho$ is the identity. The full integration functional is $\mathcal I_\rho=\ell_\rho\circ\mathcal B_\rho$, extended coefficientwise to source variables and $R_N$. Thus “integration over odd coordinates” means coefficient extraction in the chosen exterior algebra, not an ordinary integral over odd numbers.

Introduce commuting formal source variables $j_1,\ldots,j_{n_0}$ dual to the even coordinates and independent anticommuting formal source generators $\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_{n_1}$ dual to the ordered odd coordinates. Their algebra is $\mathscr J_\rho=\mathbb C[\![j_1,\ldots,j_{n_0}]\!]\otimes\Lambda(\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_{n_1})$. In these bases the source pairing is
$$
\langle J,\varphi\rangle=\sum_{a=1}^{n_0}j_aq^a+\sum_{b=1}^{n_1}\eta_b\xi_b,
$$
with each odd source placed to the left of its odd field coordinate, so the pairing is even. In particular, $J$ is a graded formal source, not an ordinary element of the complex dual $X_\rho^*$.

A regulated perturbative generating datum also specifies an even action $S_{\rho,\epsilon}\in\mathcal H_\rho\otimes R_N$ and the generating functional
$$
Z_{\rho,\epsilon}[J]=\mathcal I_\rho\!\left(\exp\!\bigl(iS_{\rho,\epsilon}(\varphi)+i\langle J,\varphi\rangle\bigr)\right),\qquad Z_{\rho,\epsilon}[0]\text{ is a unit}.
$$
The exponential is interpreted in the chosen convergent or formal algebra: the ordinary exponential is applied to the commuting body and the nilpotent odd and $\epsilon$ parts are expanded finitely. Every coefficient of the generating integrand and of its formal source derivatives must belong to the domain of $\mathcal I_\rho$. “A unit” means that the $\epsilon^0$ coefficient of $Z_{\rho,\epsilon}[0]$ is nonzero; hence the normalized functional $\widehat Z_{\rho,\epsilon}[J]=Z_{\rho,\epsilon}[J]/Z_{\rho,\epsilon}[0]$ is defined in $\mathscr J_\rho\otimes R_N$ and has constant term $1$ at $J=0$.

For an ordered list of source components, define the connected $n$-point kernel as $i^{-n}$ times the corresponding ordered source derivatives of $\log\widehat Z_{\rho,\epsilon}[J]$ at $J=0$. Even-source derivatives are ordinary derivatives. Odd-source derivatives are left graded derivatives, characterized by $\partial^L_{\eta_a}\eta_b=\delta_{ab}$ and
$$
\partial^L_{\eta_a}(UV)=(\partial^L_{\eta_a}U)V+(-1)^{|U|}U(\partial^L_{\eta_a}V)
$$
for homogeneous $U,V$. The logarithm is the formal logarithm with zero constant term. The regulator datum supplies the reconstruction of the component kernels as spacetime kernels and a Fourier-transform convention. The Fourier transform is $\widetilde f(p)=\int e^{ip\cdot x}f(x)\,d^4x$, interpreted in the specified function or distribution space.

An admissible field-coordinate change is a local, parity-preserving formal map $F_{\rho,\epsilon}=\operatorname{id}+\sum_{k=1}^{N}\epsilon^kF_{\rho,k}$ on these graded coordinates with an inverse modulo $\epsilon^{N+1}$. Each coefficient of each $F_{\rho,k}$ is polynomial in the odd coordinates and holomorphic in the even coordinates on a specified open neighborhood of the integration contour. Substitution into nilpotent even displacements uses finite Taylor expansions; the coordinate algebra and integration domain must contain every coefficient used in these substitutions and derivatives. Thus $DF$ is defined coefficientwise, with left odd derivatives and the stated ordering. If the coordinates come from spacetime fields, local means that each output field at $x$ depends on a finite jet of the input fields at $x$. Its regulated Jacobian factor $\mathcal J_{F,\rho}$ is a multiplier in the field-coordinate algebra specified by the exact graded change-of-variables identity
$$
\mathcal I_\rho(h(\varphi))=\mathcal I_\rho\!\left(h(F_{\rho,\epsilon}(\psi))\,\mathcal J_{F,\rho}(\psi)\right)
$$
for every admissible integrand $h$, with the functional extended coefficientwise over $\mathscr J_\rho\otimes R_N$. No assertion that $\mathcal J_{F,\rho}=1$ is part of the definition. In the coordinate-volume case the even functional integrates $dq^1\wedge\cdots\wedge dq^{n_0}$ over an oriented real $n_0$-dimensional contour; its contour and boundary data must satisfy this identity with the Berezinian multiplier. This is additional integration data, not an assertion for arbitrary $\nu_\rho$ or $\ell_\rho$. The Berezinian is defined algebraically: if the graded derivative has block form $DF=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}$ with $D$ invertible, then $\operatorname{Ber}(DF)=\det(A-BD^{-1}C)(\det D)^{-1}$. Here $DF\equiv I$ modulo $\epsilon$, so both diagonal blocks are invertible over the truncated algebra; empty determinants are one. For a general even functional the exact identity, including any measure-density factor, remains the requirement. In the transformed coordinates the source is $\langle J,F_{\rho,\epsilon}(\psi)\rangle$, so the field insertion remains the same named original coordinate.

An LSZ amplitude datum is an additional common regulator limit of the connected momentum-space Green functions, when that limit exists. For each external one-particle channel $a$ (with a fixed polarization component when the field has spin), the datum specifies a mass $m_a>0$ and nonzero simple-pole residue $Z_a\in\mathbb C^\times$ at $s_a=m_a^2$, where $s_a=-\eta^{\mu\nu}p_{a,\mu}p_{a,\nu}$. A stable external channel means precisely that this isolated pole exists with nonzero residue and zero width. Choose a nonzero scalar $z_a$ with $z_a^2=Z_a$ as part of the datum; throughout, $Z_a^{1/2}$ means this chosen $z_a$ and $Z_a^{-1/2}$ means $z_a^{-1}$. These choices are fixed for amplitude comparisons; no canonical complex square-root branch is assumed.

For each selected field-parity sector, supply equally long finite ordered lists of interpolating-field components $\varphi_A$ and channels $a$, and an invertible complex matrix $U=(U_{Aa})$. Define channel-coordinate insertions $\chi_a=\sum_A(U^{-1})_{aA}\varphi_A$ and their ordered connected kernels by multilinearity:
$$
G_{a_1\ldots a_n}=\sum_{A_1,\ldots,A_n}\left(\prod_{j=1}^n(U^{-1})_{a_j A_j}\right)G_{A_1\ldots A_n}.
$$
Require the following external-leg pole factorization for the original component kernels:
$$
G_{A_1\ldots A_n}=\sum_{b_1,\ldots,b_n}\left(\prod_{j=1}^n\frac{U_{A_j b_j}z_{b_j}}{s_j-m_{b_j}^2}\right)\mathcal A_{b_1\ldots b_n}+\text{terms missing at least one external pole}.
$$
The sums run over the declared channels in the corresponding parity sectors, and every remainder must have zero joint residue at every declared external-pole tuple. This equation defines the overlap meaning of $U$: the external-leg factor of $\varphi_A$ for channel $a$ is $U_{Aa}z_a$. Multiplying by $U^{-1}$ on each leg selects its channel factor, also when channel masses coincide. Below $G_n$ abbreviates the channel-coordinate kernel $G_{a_1\ldots a_n}$. Require its pole factorization
$$
G_n(p_1,\ldots,p_n)=\left(\prod_{j=1}^n\frac{Z_{a_j}^{1/2}}{s_j-m_{a_j}^2}\right)\mathcal A_n(p_1,\ldots,p_n)+\text{terms missing at least one external pole}.
$$
The normalized LSZ amplitude is the joint residue
$$
\mathcal A_n=\left(\prod_{j=1}^n Z_{a_j}^{-1/2}\right)\lim_{s_j\to m_{a_j}^2}\left(\prod_{j=1}^n(s_j-m_{a_j}^2)\right)G_n,
$$
with the overall momentum-conservation delta function removed and the same ordered graded-source convention as above. The joint limits, Fourier transforms, pole factorization and invertible overlap data must all exist as part of the supplied LSZ datum. This definition supplies only the regulator and pole data needed for a conditional amplitude statement. It does not assert that a continuum limit, stable particles, or LSZ poles exist for a given quantum field theory.

derivations.claim: Fix $\rho$ and apply A2 to $h(\varphi)=\exp(iS_{\rho,\epsilon}(\varphi)+i\langle J,\varphi\rangle)$. By F1 this generating integrand and its graded source derivatives lie in the domain of $\mathcal I_\rho$, so the exact identity gives $Z'_{\rho,\epsilon}[J]=Z_{\rho,\epsilon}[J]$ coefficientwise in $R_N$.

At $J=0$ the partition values are equal by step 1.1 and are units by hypothesis. Division by this common unit shows that the normalized source functionals agree in the graded source algebra over $R_N$.

Taking the formal logarithms of the equal normalized functionals in step 2.1 and then applying the same ordered left graded source derivatives gives equal connected Green functions for the original fields and for the transformed insertions $F_{\rho,\epsilon}(\psi)$. The supplied Fourier transform and removal of the same momentum-conservation delta function preserve equality. Passing to the common regulator limit preserves equality wherever that limit exists.

The LSZ amplitudes are the normalized joint residues of these connected functions. By step 3.1 the component functions agree; applying the same $U^{-1}$ on each external leg gives equal channel-coordinate kernels. Their joint residues agree, and multiplication by the same fixed $z_{a_j}^{-1}$ gives equal normalized amplitudes coefficientwise through order $N$. If any required common limit or stable pole does not exist, the corresponding amplitude conclusion is not asserted.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Use natural units $c=\hbar=1$ on four-dimensional Minkowski space $M=\mathbb R^{1,3}$ with coordinates $x^0=ct,x^1,x^2,x^3$ and metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. Fix a complex affine algebraic group $G$ with no nontrivial closed normal unipotent subgroup, where unipotent means that every nonzero finite-dimensional rational module has a nonzero fixed vector; this is the reductive hypothesis. Fix a finite set $I$ of field species. For each $i\in I$, fix a finite-dimensional complex $\mathbb Z/2$-graded vector space $\Phi_i=\Phi_i^{\bar 0}\oplus\Phi_i^{\bar 1}$ with a homogeneous basis and its component parities, and an algebraic representation $\rho_i:G\to\operatorname{GL}(\Phi_i)$ preserving the grading. Include the declared spacetime-index action in $G$ or in its specified finite-dimensional representation data.

For the field interpretation, fix a finite Grassmann coefficient algebra $\mathcal G=\Lambda_{\mathbb C}(\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_s)$, $s\geq0$, with its usual grading by generator degree modulo two. A field configuration assigns to each homogeneous component of parity $\bar p$ a function $M\to\mathcal G_{\bar p}$ whose coefficient at each exterior monomial is smooth; spacetime derivatives are taken coefficientwise. Evaluation of a polynomial on an $r$-jet means the parity-preserving algebra homomorphism that sends each polynomial coordinate to the corresponding field component or derivative at that point.

Fix a derivative cutoff $r\geq0$, a maximum polynomial field degree $q\geq0$, and a rational engineering weight $\Delta_i$ for each field species. A derivative $\partial_\mu$ has engineering weight one, and an $s$-jet generator is a component of $\partial_{\mu_1}\cdots\partial_{\mu_s}\phi_i(x)$ for $0\leq s\leq r$. If covariant derivatives are used, their finite jet generators and $G$-action are included explicitly in the same data. Let $J_r$ be the resulting finite-dimensional $\mathbb Z/2$-graded vector space with its specified algebraic representation $\rho_r:G\to\operatorname{GL}(J_r)$, required to preserve the grading and the assigned engineering weights. Its polynomial algebra is the supercommutative algebra $P_r=\operatorname{Sym}(J_{r,\bar 0}^{*})\otimes\Lambda(J_{r,\bar 1}^{*})$: even generators commute and odd generators anticommute. The induced left $G$-action on $P_r$ is $(g\cdot f)(z)=f(\rho_r(g^{-1})z)$ for $g\in G$, $f\in P_r$, and $z\in J_r$. For a fixed weight $D\in\mathbb Q$, let $P_{r,q,D}$ be the complex span of monomials of total engineering weight $D$ and total polynomial degree at most $q$.

A local operator in this finite-order data is an element of $P_{r,q,D}$ evaluated at $x$ on the $r$-jet of the fields. A scalar operator invariant under the declared symmetries is an element of $V_{r,q,D}=P_{r,q,D}^{G}$. Engineering dimension means this assigned mass weight; it is not a statement about an observed quantity. In four dimensions a term with operator $\mathcal O_D$ has the convention $C\mathcal O_D/\Lambda^{D-4}$, where $\Lambda$ has mass dimension one and $C$ is dimensionless. Reality conditions, when required for a real action, are additional conjugation data on $V_{r,q,D}$.

Fix a finite jet order $r$, maximum polynomial field degree $q$, engineering weight $D$, finite field-species list, coefficient field $\mathbb C$, and complex reductive affine algebraic group $G$ with the finite-dimensional rational action specified on the jet generators, including the declared spacetime-index symmetries. Let $W_D$ be the finite-dimensional space of all local polynomials of weight $D$ and degree at most $q$, before imposing $G$-invariance, and let $V_D=W_D^G$ be its invariant scalar subspace. An admitted raw relation space is a specified $G$-stable linear subspace $\widetilde R_D\leq W_D$, given by explicit linear identities among the chosen polynomials. Its invariant part is $R_D=\widetilde R_D\cap V_D$. Any action, boundary, or observable interpretation of the selected identities is extra mathematical data and must be stated with the result that verifies it.

The finite-order invariant operator-basis quotient is

$$
\mathcal Q_D:=V_D/R_D.
$$

Two invariant operators represent the same class exactly when their difference lies in $R_D$. An operator basis is any finite list of representatives in $V_D$ of a vector-space basis of $\mathcal Q_D$. The quotient records precisely the declared relation space; it does not assert that every relation relevant to an arbitrary EFT, observable, or infinite operator tower has been included.

Assume full AC. Use four-dimensional natural units $c=\hbar=1$ and a finite jet-polynomial field model with its declared finite rational action of a complex reductive affine algebraic group $G$. Let $W_D$ be a finite raw local-polynomial space at fixed engineering weight $D$, derivative cutoff, and field-degree cutoff; let $V_D=W_D^G$. Let $\widetilde R_D$ be the $G$-stable linear span in $W_D$ of the declared polynomial identities, admitted total-divergence densities, and leading-equation densities $F^a\mathcal E_a^{(0)}$ defined below, with $R_D=\widetilde R_D\cap V_D$. The finite-order invariant operator quotient is $\mathcal Q_D=V_D/R_D$.

Let $M=\mathbb R^{1,3}$ with $x^0=ct$, $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and volume measure $d^4x$. Even field components are smooth maps $M\to\Phi_a^{\bar0}$ and odd components are smooth coefficient families in a fixed Grassmann algebra valued in $\Phi_a^{\bar1}$; admitted variations and currents have compact support. Let $\mathcal I[L]=\int_M L\,d^4x$ on admitted local densities, with the boundary convention $\mathcal I(\partial_\mu J^\mu)=0$. Let $S_0[\phi]$ and each $S_j[\phi]$ be $G$-invariant local polynomial functionals of these field configurations, so their formal Taylor expansions through order $N$ are defined. Let the variational derivative $\mathcal E_a^{(0)}[\phi]$ of $S_0$ be defined by

$$
D S_0[\phi](h)=\mathcal I\!\left(\sum_a h^a\mathcal E_a^{(0)}[\phi]\right)
$$

for every admitted compactly supported parity-compatible variation $h$. A leading-equation relation is a density $F^a\mathcal E_a^{(0)}$ with $F^a[\phi]$ a smooth function of $x$ and finitely many component jets of $\phi$ at $x$, with this density in $W_D$, and satisfying the following conditions: its component parity matches that of $\phi^a$; it is $G$-equivariant, meaning $F[g\cdot\phi]=g\cdot F[\phi]$; and it preserves compact support, meaning $\operatorname{supp}F[\phi]\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\phi$ for compactly supported $\phi$. At each configuration where the action identities below are applied, require $F[\phi]$ itself to be an admitted compactly supported variation, so the stated first-variation identity applies to this direction. An integration-by-parts relation is a density $\partial_\mu J^\mu$ satisfying the stated boundary convention. Consider a finite formal action $S_\epsilon=S_0+\sum_{j=1}^N\epsilon^jS_j$ in the ring $\mathbb C[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^{N+1})$, where $\epsilon$ is dimensionless and each $\epsilon^kF^a$ has the units of $\phi^a$. For every $1\leq k\leq N$, the local identity-leading change of variables $\Psi_k(\phi)=\phi-\epsilon^kF[\phi]$ is invertible as a formal map through order $N$ and satisfies

$$
S_\epsilon[\Psi_k(\phi)]=S_\epsilon[\phi]-\epsilon^k\mathcal I\!\left(F^a\mathcal E_a^{(0)}[\phi]\right)+O(\epsilon^{k+1}).
$$

Thus a coefficient $+\epsilon^k\mathcal I(F^a\mathcal E_a^{(0)})$ can be removed at order $k$ without changing lower-order coefficients, provided all induced terms through the retained order are kept. The quotient $\mathcal Q_D$ identifies exactly the declared polynomial, boundary, and leading-equation relation span; it asserts no equivalence of arbitrary off-shell Green functions and does not by itself assert a quantum measure or amplitude equivalence.

derivations.claim: For a compactly supported variation $h$, the kinetic variation is $-\mathcal I(\partial_\mu h\,\partial^\mu\phi)=\mathcal I(h\Box\phi)$, since $\partial_\mu(h\partial^\mu\phi)$ integrates to zero. The potential variation is $\mathcal I(h(-m^2\phi-g\phi^3/6))$. Thus $DS_0[\phi](h)=\mathcal I(h\mathcal E_0)$ with the displayed $\mathcal E_0$.

The field has weight one and each derivative has weight one, so $\mathcal O_6$ has weight six; $M_s^2\phi^4$ and $g\phi^6$ also have weight six. Their derivative orders and field degrees lie within the stated cutoffs, so the displayed identity concerns elements of the declared finite operator space.

The product rule gives $\partial_\mu(\phi^3\partial^\mu\phi)=3\phi^2\partial_\mu\phi\partial^\mu\phi+\phi^3\Box\phi$. The boundary convention therefore yields $\mathcal I(\phi^3\Box\phi)=-3\mathcal I(\mathcal O_6)$.

Before specialization, substituting $\widehat{\mathcal E}_0=\Box\phi-M_s^2\phi-g\phi^3/6$ into step 1.3 gives $\mathcal I(\phi^3\widehat{\mathcal E}_0)=-3\mathcal I(\mathcal O_6)-\mathcal I(M_s^2\phi^4)-(g/6)\mathcal I(\phi^6)$. Each density has weight six, and the relation subspace contains this leading-equation density and the divergence from step 1.3. The quotient definition [F2] therefore gives the displayed class identity.

Put $a=C/(3\Lambda^2)$ and use [F3] with $k=1$ and $F[\phi]=-a\phi^3$, so its map $\phi-\epsilon F[\phi]$ is $\phi+\epsilon a\phi^3$. Its units are those of $\phi$, and its first-order action change is $-\epsilon\mathcal I(F\mathcal E_0)=\epsilon a\mathcal I(\phi^3\mathcal E_0)$, as also follows from step 1.1. Since $\epsilon^2=0$, substituting the shifted field into the order-$\epsilon$ term changes that term only by zero in the truncated ring.

Specialize $M_s=m$ in step 2.1, insert that identity into step 2.2, and add the original $+\epsilon(C/\Lambda^2)\mathcal I(\mathcal O_6)$ term. Its coefficient cancels because $3a=C/\Lambda^2$, leaving exactly the quartic and sextic shifts displayed in the Example.

With a=C/(3Λ^2), the order-epsilon coefficient is C/Λ^2-3a=0, and the remaining coefficients are -am^2 and -ag/6.
